title: Students’ Feedback Requests and Interactions with the SCRIPT Chatbot: Do They Get What They Ask For?
extended_summary:
This paper examines how novice programming students interact with a generative AI chatbot and whether the feedback they receive matches what they ask for. The authors focus on a key design problem in AI-supported programming education: how to provide flexible, helpful, pedagogically guided assistance without simply giving away full solutions. Their research questions address students’ interaction patterns with the tool, the alignment between student requests and chatbot responses, and the extent to which the chatbot follows its instructional constraints.

The intervention studied is SCRIPT, a web-based chatbot built on ChatGPT-4o-mini for introductory programming support. SCRIPT offers two modes of prompting: predefined closed prompts aligned with a programming feedback typology, and open-ended prompts where students can ask free-form questions. The system includes task descriptions and reference solutions in the prompt context, and it is designed to provide step-by-step guidance, examples, and code templates while avoiding full code solutions. The authors analyzed 241 chat sessions comprising 1,409 student prompts and 1,409 chatbot responses, using structured coding of feedback types and additional interaction categories, along with quantitative counts of matches, mismatches, correctness, and adherence to system constraints.

The study was conducted with 136 students in an introductory programming course for first-year computing students at Goethe University Frankfurt in Germany during winter term 2024/25. Students used SCRIPT voluntarily at home to solve three programming tasks over approximately one week, in an unsupervised, self-paced context connected to the course Moodle site. The participants were primarily undergraduate computer science students, and no prior programming experience was required.

The main conclusions are that students appeared to follow a recurring sequence of feedback needs, moving from understanding task constraints and concepts to next steps, debugging, evaluating correctness, and finally seeking correct solutions. SCRIPT’s responses matched or over-matched students’ requested feedback types in 75% of evaluated prompt-response pairs, and 81% of analyzed responses were judged fully correct. The chatbot generally adhered to pedagogical guardrails, but it sometimes provided multiple steps at once, completed templates over repeated interactions, or gave solutions earlier than intended. The authors conclude that combining structured and open prompting can support novice programmers effectively, while also highlighting the continuing challenge of balancing guidance, flexibility, and restriction in AI tutoring tools.

identified_tools.name: SCRIPT
identified_tools.description: A standalone web-based supportive chatbot for resolving introductory programming tasks, built on ChatGPT and designed for novice programmers with both predefined feedback prompts and open-ended interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a GenAI chatbot in an introductory programming course to support students solving programming exercises, focusing on the types of feedback students requested, how well responses matched those requests, and whether outputs adhered to pedagogical/system constraints.

findings.finding_summary: In an experiment with 136 students, SCRIPT’s responses aligned with students’ requested feedback types in 75% of evaluated question-response pairs when direct matches and over-matches were combined (47% direct matches: 417/891 pairs; plus 255/891 over-matches). Mismatches occurred in 22% of pairs (195/891), and 25% of those mismatches (49/195) were direct-solution requests that SCRIPT was intentionally designed to reject.
findings.measure: Alignment between student feedback requests and SCRIPT response types across coded question-response pairs

findings.finding_summary: Across 1,016 problem-related responses, SCRIPT’s response correctness was high: 81% were fully correct, 14% partially correct, and 5% incorrect. Students also provided 151 thumbs ratings, of which 130 were positive and 21 negative, with positive comments emphasizing clear explanations and helpful guidance.
findings.measure: Coded correctness of chatbot responses and student ratings of responses

findings.finding_summary: Regarding adherence to pedagogical constraints, 51% of problem-related responses provided a single step as intended, while 21% included multiple steps but with an explicit next step and 28% included multiple steps. SCRIPT provided solutions in 42 of 100 direct correct-solution requests, generated 167 intended templates but also 95 completed templates, and directly corrected student code 34 times despite the constraint not to do so.
findings.measure: Adherence to system-prompt constraints for stepwise guidance, solution withholding, template generation, and code correction
findings.effect_size: 51% single-step; 42/100 solutions given; 167 templates provided; 95 completed templates; 34 code corrections

findings.finding_summary: Analysis of 241 chat sessions and 1,409 prompts showed students tended to follow a recurring feedback-seeking sequence: task constraints (KTC), concepts (KC), how to proceed (KH), mistakes (KM), performance/result checking (KP/KR), and then correct solution requests (KCR). The chatbot supported iterative help-seeking and clarification, but some students used repeated next-step requests to incrementally reconstruct solutions.
findings.measure: Observed student interaction patterns and feedback-seeking sequences in chat logs

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical study of a specific named chatbot with substantial log data from 136 students, but it is primarily descriptive/qualitative coding and system-evaluation rather than an RCT or strong causal design on student learning gains.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive alignment and correctness metrics for the tool, but does not provide standardized effect sizes or direct evidence of improved academic achievement, so educational impact remains promising but unclear.
